newsitem.title: GERMANY: Situation in flood-hit east Germany still critical.
newsitem.headline: Situation in flood-hit east Germany still critical.

text.p: Flood barriers were still under huge pressure from the swollen River Oder on Friday, despite massive overnight repair efforts by thousands of German soldiers to prevent the area being submerged.

Military personnel, aid workers and villagers patched up dikes protecting the low-lying Oderbruch area on the Polish border that had crumbled under the weight of two weeks of floods. But more weak spots appeared in other places.
"We were working all night, but the situation remains critical," an Army press spokesman told ARD television.
Around 15,000 people were evacuated from the region since last week and thousands more have been warned to be ready to leave their homes at a moment's notice.

As the struggle raged to contain the floods on both sides of the river Oder dividing Germany and Poland, talks were already under way between the two on a joint project with European Union support to prevent this happening again.

European Commissioner Monika Wulf-Mathies, responsible for regional aid projects, was scheduled to pay a visit later in the day to Hohenwutzen in east Germany, where soldiers and aid workers have been fighting to prevent a breach in the dike.

The visit comes just a day after Manfred Stolpe, premier of Brandenburg state, and Polish Interior Minister Leszek Miller proposed a joint project with assistance from the EU to modernise dikes and other infrastructure along the Oder river.
If approved, the project could involve large sums of money and transform the flood catastrophe into a programme to boost jobs in a region with above average unemployment.
"We are now assessing the damages with the help of the German and Dutch governments," Alain Pilloux of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development told CNN television.
"In the end I think there will be enough money to mitigate the effects of the floods."

Poland and the Czech Republic have been hit hard by Europe's worst floods in over a century that have claimed over 100 lives and inundated the Polish cities of Wroclaw and Opole, leaving tens of thousands of people homeless.
Along Germany's eastern border floods have not caused any deaths, but there has been extensive damage to homes, businesses, factories and local infrastructure.

Several towns are completely under water near Frankfurt an der Oder, around 70 km (40 miles) from Berlin, and the Bonn government and the state of Brandenburg have agreed a 40 million-mark ($22 million) emergeny aid fund to provide immediate assistance to flood victims.
The Polish government estimates damage from the floods could be as high as $1.4 billion, and German officials have put the cost to their country at around one billion marks.

Stolpe and Miller gave no details of their aid proposals, but it appears the plan would go beyond aid for victims and tap EU funds for regional development that could improve facilities and boost economic ties along the Oder.

"The plan would encompass various goals -- the Oder River as a transport route, environment protection, water retention reservoirs and dams which would protect cities along the river," Miller said on Thursday.
"There is a chance for a European-scale project for the Oder," Stolpe said, adding EU officials had reacted positively to the idea.

European Commissioner Emma Bonino is touring the region this week and has said her humanitarian aid office would give more assistance if needed for the flood-stricken areas of the Czech Republic and Poland. The Commission has already provided 2.5 million ECU ($2.7 million) for the flooded areas.

In the Czech Republic homes have been wrecked, crops destroyed and road, rail and telecommunications links have been severed. Economists have said damage could be as high as $2.6 billion, but it is still too soon to say.
